quests.sentenceWithBlank: Maria packed her backpack ____ she put on her hiking boots.
quests.completedSentence: Maria packed her backpack and she put on her hiking boots.
quests.ruleExplanation: 'And' links two ordinary steps in getting ready. Putting on her boots isn't a result of packing the backpack, so 'so' doesn't fit here, and there's no contrast for 'but' or choice for 'or' - both actions just happen together.
quests.nativeTip: Think about whether the second action simply follows the first as another step, without any surprise or cause-and-effect.
quests.example: Maria packed her backpack and she put on her hiking boots.

quests.sentenceWithBlank: Ben packed his suitcase ____ he checked his passport twice.
quests.completedSentence: Ben packed his suitcase and he checked his passport twice.
quests.grammarRule: Addition vs Result - and, not so
quests.ruleExplanation: 'And' simply adds a second action without implying that packing caused the passport check. 'So' would wrongly suggest the check happened because of the packing - really both are just separate pre-trip tasks.
quests.nativeTip: Ask whether the second action was caused by the first, or was just another thing he did before the trip.
quests.example: Ben packed his suitcase and he checked his passport twice.

quests.sentenceWithBlank: Tom updated the spreadsheet ____ shared it with the marketing team.
quests.completedSentence: Tom updated the spreadsheet and shared it with the marketing team.
quests.ruleExplanation: 'And' connects two related actions Tom completed one after the other. 'Or' would wrongly suggest he only did one of the two, and 'but' would suggest some conflict between updating and sharing, which isn't present here.
quests.nativeTip: Both actions are steps he took in order, not a contrast or a choice between them.
quests.example: Tom updated the spreadsheet and shared it with the marketing team.

quests.sentenceWithBlank: Lily studied all weekend ____ still failed the quiz.
quests.completedSentence: Lily studied all weekend but still failed the quiz.
quests.ruleExplanation: 'But' signals a contrast between two ideas. Despite studying hard, the outcome was negative. 'So' would only work if failing were a logical result of studying, which contradicts what actually happened.
quests.nativeTip: The result is the opposite of what you'd expect after all that effort.
quests.example: Lily studied all weekend but still failed the quiz.

quests.sentenceWithBlank: The jacket was expensive ____ Nina bought it anyway.
quests.completedSentence: The jacket was expensive but Nina bought it anyway.
quests.ruleExplanation: 'But' introduces contrast: the price might have stopped her, yet she bought it. 'And' would only add information without showing this contradiction, and 'so' would wrongly suggest the price was the reason she bought it.
quests.nativeTip: Notice the word 'anyway' - it signals she acted against what the first clause suggests.
quests.example: The jacket was expensive but Nina bought it anyway.

quests.sentenceWithBlank: Carlos wanted to relax after work ____ his neighbor asked for help moving furniture.
quests.completedSentence: Carlos wanted to relax after work but his neighbor asked for help moving furniture.
quests.ruleExplanation: 'But' shows the neighbor's request goes against what Carlos wanted to do. 'And' would just list two unrelated facts, missing the sense that his plan was disrupted.
quests.nativeTip: One plan gets interrupted by something unwanted, rather than simply added to it.
quests.example: Carlos wanted to relax after work but his neighbor asked for help moving furniture.

quests.sentenceWithBlank: You can order the soup ____ the salad as your starter.
quests.completedSentence: You can order the soup or the salad as your starter.
quests.ruleExplanation: 'Or' presents a choice between two starters, matching the singular 'your starter.' 'And' would mean ordering both together, which doesn't match a single starter.
quests.nativeTip: The sentence says 'your starter,' singular - only one of these two dishes is being chosen.
quests.example: You can order the soup or the salad as your starter.

quests.sentenceWithBlank: You can pay by card ____ cash at the counter.
quests.completedSentence: You can pay by card or cash at the counter.
quests.ruleExplanation: 'Or' offers a choice between two accepted payment methods. 'And' would suggest you need to use both at once, which isn't the normal meaning of this kind of sentence.
quests.nativeTip: The two payment methods are options to pick between, not something to combine.
quests.example: You can pay by card or cash at the counter.

quests.sentenceWithBlank: We could fly directly ____ save money by taking a connecting flight.
quests.completedSentence: We could fly directly or save money by taking a connecting flight.
quests.ruleExplanation: 'Or' shows two travel options being compared. 'And' doesn't work here because flying directly and taking a connecting flight are mutually exclusive - you'd choose one.
quests.nativeTip: You can't fly directly and take a connecting flight at the same time - these are two different routes to weigh against each other.
quests.example: We could fly directly or save money by taking a connecting flight.

quests.sentenceWithBlank: The storm knocked out the power ____ we lit candles for the evening.
quests.completedSentence: The storm knocked out the power so we lit candles for the evening.
quests.ruleExplanation: 'So' introduces a result. Losing power caused them to light candles. 'And' would just add the action without showing that one thing led to the other.
quests.nativeTip: The second action happens because of the situation described first.
quests.example: The storm knocked out the power so we lit candles for the evening.

quests.sentenceWithBlank: The client changed the deadline ____ the whole team had to rearrange their schedules.
quests.completedSentence: The client changed the deadline so the whole team had to rearrange their schedules.
quests.ruleExplanation: 'So' expresses that the deadline change caused the scheduling problem. 'And' would only add the second fact without showing this cause-and-effect link.
quests.nativeTip: The rearranged schedules happened directly because of the deadline change.
quests.example: The client changed the deadline so the whole team had to rearrange their schedules.

quests.sentenceWithBlank: Elena had a bad headache all day ____ she left work early.
quests.completedSentence: Elena had a bad headache all day so she left work early.
quests.ruleExplanation: 'So' shows the headache led to her decision to leave. 'And' would list the two facts without showing the cause behind her early departure.
quests.nativeTip: Leaving work is a direct consequence of how she felt, not just another fact added on.
quests.example: Elena had a bad headache all day so she left work early.

quests.sentenceWithBlank: Priya invited her whole team to the party ____ only half of them came.
quests.completedSentence: Priya invited her whole team to the party but only half of them came.
quests.grammarRule: Contrast vs Addition - but, not and
quests.ruleExplanation: 'But' marks the gap between what was expected - a full team - and what happened - only half. 'And' would just report both facts without showing that the turnout was lower than hoped.
quests.nativeTip: The outcome is smaller than what the first clause leads you to expect.
quests.example: Priya invited her whole team to the party but only half of them came.

quests.sentenceWithBlank: Sam checked his email every morning ____ replied to any urgent messages.
quests.completedSentence: Sam checked his email every morning and replied to any urgent messages.
quests.ruleExplanation: 'And' links two ordinary steps in his routine. There's no contrast, so 'but' would wrongly suggest some conflict between checking email and replying to it.
quests.nativeTip: Both actions are simply part of the same daily routine - nothing here goes against expectation.
quests.example: Sam checked his email every morning and replied to any urgent messages.

quests.sentenceWithBlank: The bill arrived a week late ____ Jason still paid it on time.
quests.completedSentence: The bill arrived a week late but Jason still paid it on time.
quests.ruleExplanation: 'But' captures the contrast between the bill arriving late and him paying on time regardless. 'So' would wrongly suggest the late arrival caused the on-time payment, which reverses the logic.
quests.nativeTip: He met the deadline anyway, despite the late arrival - that's a contradiction, not a simple addition.
quests.example: The bill arrived a week late but Jason still paid it on time.

quests.sentenceWithBlank: Ana can choose the blue sofa ____ the grey one for the living room.
quests.completedSentence: Ana can choose the blue sofa or the grey one for the living room.
quests.ruleExplanation: 'Or' shows two alternatives she must choose between. 'And' would mean buying both sofas, which doesn't match the idea of choosing.
quests.nativeTip: The word 'choose' already tells you she's picking one, not both.
quests.example: Ana can choose the blue sofa or the grey one for the living room.

quests.sentenceWithBlank: Add the flour ____ mix it in gently until smooth.
quests.completedSentence: Add the flour and mix it in gently until smooth.
quests.ruleExplanation: 'And' links two steps in the same instruction. 'Or' would wrongly suggest you only do one of the two things, when actually both are required to make the dish.
quests.nativeTip: These are two steps you do one after another, not two choices.
quests.example: Add the flour and mix it in gently until smooth.

quests.sentenceWithBlank: You can walk the dog in the morning ____ in the evening, whichever suits your schedule.
quests.completedSentence: You can walk the dog in the morning or in the evening, whichever suits your schedule.
quests.ruleExplanation: 'Or' fits because the sentence explicitly offers a choice between two times. 'And' would contradict the meaning of 'whichever,' which signals picking just one.
quests.nativeTip: The phrase 'whichever suits' tells you this is a choice, not a combination.
quests.example: You can walk the dog in the morning or in the evening, whichever suits your schedule.

quests.sentenceWithBlank: Traffic is always terrible on Monday mornings ____ Noah leaves the house an hour earlier that day.
quests.completedSentence: Traffic is always terrible on Monday mornings so Noah leaves the house an hour earlier that day.
quests.ruleExplanation: 'So' shows that the predictable Monday traffic is the reason he leaves early. 'And' would only add the second fact without explaining why he changed his schedule.
quests.nativeTip: His routine change is a response to the regular traffic pattern, not just another separate fact.
quests.example: Traffic is always terrible on Monday mornings so Noah leaves the house an hour earlier that day.

quests.sentenceWithBlank: Grace reviewed her notes every night ____ highlighted the key formulas in yellow.
quests.completedSentence: Grace reviewed her notes every night and highlighted the key formulas in yellow.
quests.ruleExplanation: 'And' adds a second habitual action without implying cause. 'So' would incorrectly suggest the highlighting happened because of the reviewing, rather than both being separate parts of her routine.
quests.nativeTip: Highlighting formulas isn't a consequence of reviewing - it's simply another study habit she has.
quests.example: Grace reviewed her notes every night and highlighted the key formulas in yellow.

quests.sentenceWithBlank: The library extended its hours for exam season ____ Ben started studying there every evening.
quests.completedSentence: The library extended its hours for exam season so Ben started studying there every evening.
quests.ruleExplanation: 'So' links the cause - extended hours - with its effect - Ben studying there more. 'And' would just add the fact without showing this cause-effect connection.
quests.nativeTip: His new evening habit is a direct effect of the library's schedule change.
quests.example: The library extended its hours for exam season so Ben started studying there every evening.

quests.sentenceWithBlank: The flight was fully booked ____ Maria managed to get a seat on standby.
quests.completedSentence: The flight was fully booked but Maria managed to get a seat on standby.
quests.grammarRule: Contrast vs Result - but, not so
quests.ruleExplanation: 'But' shows contrast: being fully booked would normally mean no seats, yet she got one anyway. 'So' would wrongly suggest the full booking caused her to get a seat, which doesn't make sense.
quests.nativeTip: She succeeded even though the situation seemed to rule it out - that's a contradiction, not a cause.
quests.example: The flight was fully booked but Maria managed to get a seat on standby.

quests.sentenceWithBlank: The printer ran out of ink ____ Tom had to email the document instead.
quests.completedSentence: The printer ran out of ink so Tom had to email the document instead.
quests.ruleExplanation: 'So' shows the ink shortage caused him to change his plan. 'But' would only fit if emailing the document went against the ink problem somehow, which it doesn't - it's the logical response.
quests.nativeTip: Emailing instead is a direct consequence of the ink running out, not a contradiction.
quests.example: The printer ran out of ink so Tom had to email the document instead.

quests.sentenceWithBlank: The rain didn't stop all afternoon ____ the wedding photos were taken indoors instead.
quests.completedSentence: The rain didn't stop all afternoon so the wedding photos were taken indoors instead.
quests.ruleExplanation: 'So' connects the cause - nonstop rain - with the practical result of moving the photos indoors. 'But' would suggest the indoor photos happened despite something, which isn't the relationship here.
quests.nativeTip: The location change is a practical response to the rain, not a surprising contradiction.
quests.example: The rain didn't stop all afternoon so the wedding photos were taken indoors instead.

quests.sentenceWithBlank: The moving truck arrived late ____ the movers still finished loading everything by noon.
quests.completedSentence: The moving truck arrived late but the movers still finished loading everything by noon.
quests.ruleExplanation: 'But' highlights the contrast between the late start and the on-time finish, reinforced by the word 'still.' 'So' would incorrectly suggest the late arrival caused them to finish on time.
quests.nativeTip: Finishing on time despite the late start goes against what you'd expect.
quests.example: The moving truck arrived late but the movers still finished loading everything by noon.

quests.sentenceWithBlank: To back up your photos, you can use the cloud ____ an external drive - either option keeps them safe.
quests.completedSentence: To back up your photos, you can use the cloud or an external drive - either option keeps them safe.
quests.ruleExplanation: 'Or' presents two alternative backup methods, matching 'either option.' 'And' would suggest doing both together, which changes the meaning from choosing a method to combining them.
quests.nativeTip: The phrase 'either option' tells you a single method is enough - this isn't about combining both.
quests.example: To back up your photos, you can use the cloud or an external drive - either option keeps them safe.

quests.sentenceWithBlank: Nina hadn't slept well for days ____ she finally booked a doctor's appointment.
quests.completedSentence: Nina hadn't slept well for days so she finally booked a doctor's appointment.
quests.ruleExplanation: 'So' connects the lack of sleep as the cause with her decision to see a doctor as the result. 'And' would list the two facts without showing this cause-effect link.
quests.nativeTip: Booking the appointment is a direct response to the ongoing problem, not just another unrelated fact.
quests.example: Nina hadn't slept well for days so she finally booked a doctor's appointment.

quests.sentenceWithBlank: The train was cancelled ____ Carlos decided to drive to the city instead.
quests.completedSentence: The train was cancelled so Carlos decided to drive to the city instead.
quests.ruleExplanation: 'So' shows the cancellation directly led to his decision to drive. 'But' would suggest his driving somehow contradicted the cancellation, which isn't the case here.
quests.nativeTip: Driving instead is what he chose to do because of the cancellation.
quests.example: The train was cancelled so Carlos decided to drive to the city instead.

quests.sentenceWithBlank: For dinner tonight, we could order pizza ____ cook something simple at home.
quests.completedSentence: For dinner tonight, we could order pizza or cook something simple at home.
quests.ruleExplanation: 'Or' shows two dinner options being weighed against each other. 'And' would mean doing both - ordering pizza and cooking - which isn't the natural reading of this sentence.
quests.nativeTip: These are two different plans for dinner - you'd pick one, not necessarily do both.
quests.example: For dinner tonight, we could order pizza or cook something simple at home.

quests.sentenceWithBlank: Jason cleaned out his inbox ____ organized his files before the long weekend.
quests.completedSentence: Jason cleaned out his inbox and organized his files before the long weekend.
quests.ruleExplanation: 'And' links two ordinary tasks he completed together before his break. There's no contrast or consequence here, just two related actions on his to-do list.
quests.nativeTip: Both tasks are simply part of the same tidy-up, with nothing unexpected or conditional between them.
quests.example: Jason cleaned out his inbox and organized his files before the long weekend.
